topics: 🐴 Five Gentile Arrangements — buyer, seller, partner, receiver, and receivership-giver of a donkey fetus, all exempt from firstborn status
❓ Why All Five Cases? — the Gemara shows each teaches something the others don't
🗡️ Selling a Broken Animal — Rabbi Yehuda permits selling a damaged (שבורה) animal to a gentile; does that extend to a fetus?
💰 The Receivership Penalty — Rabbi Yehuda's baraita: half value redeemed vs. ten times value forfeited
🐮 Selling 'For Its Fetuses' — a dilemma when the mother stays with the Jew and only future offspring are sold
⚖️ 'Whenever the Gentile's Hand Is Involved' — the Rabbis' governing principle exempting from firstborn status

overview.title: 📖 Overview: The Firstborn Donkey Belongs to a Jew Alone
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 2a–2b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Masechet Bekhorot opens not with the firstborns of kosher animals but with the firstborn donkey (פֶּטֶר חֲמוֹר), which its owner must redeem with a lamb or whose neck he must break. The very first mishna teaches that this obligation applies only when the donkey belongs entirely to a Jew: if a gentile has any share in it — through purchase, sale, partnership, receivership, or care-taking — the donkey is fully exempt, based on the verse 'I sanctified to Me all the firstborn in Israel' (Numbers 3:13). The Gemara first shows why the mishna needed all five scenarios rather than one, then pursues a related question raised elsewhere in Shas: does Rabbi Yehuda, who permits selling a damaged animal to a gentile, also permit selling an unborn fetus, or even an animal sold 'for its fetuses' alone?

slides.title: 🐴 The Mishna's Five Cases — Why Each Is Needed
slides.subtitle: Every scenario in the mishna teaches something the others could not
rows: Otherwise I'd think it's exempt only because the Jew brings the fetus into sanctity
Teaches he is not penalized for removing the fetus from sanctity, even though the sale itself is forbidden
Excludes Rabbi Yehuda's view that a gentile partnership animal is obligated in firstborn status
Stated mainly to set up the parallel case that follows
Teaches he is not penalized, lest this be confused with a case where the gentile has no rights to the offspring

callout.label: The verse:
callout.text: "I sanctified to Me all the firstborn in Israel, both man and animal" (Numbers 3:13) — the mitzva applies only to Jews, so any gentile share exempts the animal.

slides.title: 🗡️ Does 'Broken' Include a Fetus?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yehuda permits selling a damaged animal to a gentile — what about an unborn one?

lines.speaker: Dilemma
lines.text: Rabbi Yehuda permits selling a broken (שְׁבוּרָה) animal to a gentile, since it can't work. A fetus also can't work — does his leniency extend to it?

lines.speaker: Or not
lines.text: Or is a broken animal different? That's not its natural state. A fetus's incapacity is natural and temporary — it will grow to work.

lines.speaker: Proof?
lines.text: Come and hear: the mishna says the seller acted without permission, and does not exempt Rabbi Yehuda from that ruling — so he must agree it's forbidden!

lines.speaker: Rejected
lines.text: But the mishna also doesn't exempt Rabbi Yehuda from the partnership case — yet we know from a baraita that he disputes it. The mishna simply omits his view throughout.

lines.speaker: Rav Ashi
lines.text: Come and hear instead: Rabbi Yehuda permits a broken animal specifically because it cannot be cured — implying a curable animal is forbidden.

lines.speaker: Conclusion
lines.text: שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ — a fetus will eventually be able to work, so it counts as curable. Learn from this that Rabbi Yehuda forbids selling a fetus to a gentile.

callout.label: Result:
callout.text: Rabbi Yehuda's leniency for a damaged animal does not extend to an unborn fetus.

slides.title: 🐮 Selling an Animal 'For Its Fetuses'
slides.subtitle: A new dilemma: the Jew keeps the mother, sells only rights to her future offspring

nodes.content: ❓ A Jew sells a gentile only the rights to an animal's future offspring, keeping the animal itself. Permitted?

columns.label: Rabbi Yehuda's side
columns.content: Maybe he permits only a broken animal (visibly distinct, no confusion) but forbids this sale — or the opposite: since the mother never leaves the Jew's hand, all the more permitted

columns.label: The Rabbis' side
columns.content: Maybe they forbid only selling a broken animal (it visibly leaves him) but permit this sale — or the opposite: the risk of confusion with a full sale is even greater here

nodes.content: ⚖️ Both dilemmas are raised but left unresolved in our sugya

callout.label: Note:
callout.text: The Gemara raises the identical structural question for both Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis, and answers neither.

slides.title: 💰 Rabbi Yehuda's Baraita: Two Very Different Penalties
slides.subtitle: Same firstborn donkey, opposite outcomes depending on who acted improperly

boxes.title: Received From a Gentile (מְקַבֵּל)
items: A permitted arrangement — the Jew cares for the gentile's animal in exchange for a share of offspring
If it bears a firstborn: assess its value
The Jew gives half its value to the priest

boxes.title: Given in Receivership (נוֹתֵן בְּקַבָּלָה)
items: Prohibited — the Jew hands his own animal to a gentile
The Sages penalize him: buy out the gentile's share for up to ten times its value
He gives the entire value to the priest

boxes.title: Gemara's Fix
items: The penalty text (דָּמָיו) is emended to the feminine (דָּמֶיהָ) — it targets the animal, not the fetus
Case: a pregnant animal given to a gentile just to fatten it
Since we penalize for the animal, we penalize for its fetus too

callout.label: Big idea:
callout.text: Acting within a permitted structure costs half the value; violating the prohibition against entrusting an animal to a gentile costs everything.

slides.title: 🐐 Rabbi Yehuda's Real Reason for the Leniency
slides.subtitle: The Rabbis press him: doesn't a broken animal still give birth?

steps.content: 1️⃣ The Rabbis object: you permit selling a broken animal, but don't they breed it with a male, and it still gives birth to gentile-owned offspring?
2️⃣ That would suggest the Rabbis' true objection is the future offspring — so they should also forbid a fetuses-only sale
3️⃣ Gemara clarifies: the Rabbis' actual concern is confusion with a full sale of a healthy animal, not the offspring itself
4️⃣ Rabbi Yehuda's own answer: he permits a broken animal because it is 'as good as sold for slaughter' — and practically, a broken animal does not accept a male, so this concern rarely arises

callout.label: Closing line:
callout.text: The Rabbis' governing rule: כׇּל זְמַן שֶׁיַּד הַגּוֹי בָּאֶמְצַע — פְּטוּרָה מִן הַבְּכוֹרָה — whenever a gentile's hand is involved at all, the animal is exempt from firstborn status.

summary.principle: A firstborn donkey is obligated only when it belongs entirely to a Jew; any gentile share exempts it — but a Jew may not lawfully sell, entrust, or partner his animal (or its fetus) to a gentile in the first place.

flowSteps.content: 🐴 Mishna: buyer, seller, partner, receiver, and receivership-giver of a donkey fetus with a gentile — all exempt from firstborn status
❓ Gemara: why state all five cases? Each teaches something the others cannot (e.g., no penalty despite a forbidden sale)

columns.content: 🗡️ R' Yehuda permits selling a broken animal (uncurable) — but forbids a fetus, which will eventually work
🐮 Selling only future offspring, keeping the mother — left unresolved for both R' Yehuda and the Rabbis

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: whenever a gentile's hand is involved at all in ownership, the animal is exempt from firstborn status

quiz.q: According to the mishna, what verse explains why a firstborn donkey owned partly by a gentile is exempt from firstborn status?
o: "I sanctified to Me all the firstborn in Israel, both man and animal" (Numbers 3:13)
"Six days shall you labor" (Exodus 20:9)
"An eye for an eye" (Exodus 21:24)
"You shall not muzzle an ox" (Deuteronomy 25:4)
quiz.e: The mishna reads 'in Israel' as limiting the obligation to animals owned entirely by Jews — 'but not others,' i.e., not when a gentile has any share.

quiz.q: Why does the Gemara say the mishna needs to state the case of the seller (מוֹכֵר), even though selling a large animal to a gentile is generally forbidden?
o: To teach that the sale is actually permitted
To teach that the seller is not penalized with firstborn obligation despite acting improperly
To teach that gentiles may never own donkeys
To teach that the buyer must return the fetus
quiz.e: One might think the Sages would penalize the seller for removing the fetus from sanctity by imposing firstborn status anyway; the mishna teaches he is not penalized.

quiz.q: Why does the mishna need to mention the case of a partnership (מִשְׁתַּתֵּף) with a gentile?
o: To teach that partnerships with gentiles are always forbidden
To exclude Rabbi Yehuda's opinion that an animal owned in partnership with a gentile is obligated in firstborn status
To teach that the gentile must be paid first
It is unnecessary and redundant
quiz.e: Rabbi Yehuda holds that a gentile partnership animal remains obligated; the mishna's case teaches that, according to the accepted view, it is exempt.

quiz.q: In Rabbi Yehuda's baraita, what is the penalty when a Jew improperly gives his own donkey to a gentile in receivership (rather than properly receiving one from a gentile)?
o: No penalty at all
He gives half its value to the priest
He must buy out the gentile's share for up to ten times its value and give the entire value to the priest
The gentile keeps the whole animal
quiz.e: Properly receiving an animal from a gentile costs only half its value to the priest; improperly giving one's own animal to a gentile is penalized at up to ten times its value, given entirely to the priest.

quiz.q: According to Rav Ashi's proof, why does Rabbi Yehuda forbid selling a fetus to a gentile even though he permits selling a damaged (broken) animal?
o: Because fetuses are worth more money
Because he permits a broken animal only since it 'cannot be cured,' implying a curable animal is forbidden — and a fetus will eventually be able to work
Because gentiles are not allowed to own fetuses under any circumstances
Because the mishna explicitly says so
quiz.e: Rabbi Yehuda's stated reason for permitting the sale of a broken animal is that it cannot be cured to work again; a fetus, which will eventually be capable of work, is therefore treated as curable and forbidden to sell.
